tip: After 'de', the adjective takes -e: 'vers' becomes 'verse' in 'de verse groenten'.
Dutch drops the article here: it is 'naar school', not 'naar de school', like English 'to school'.
'Vergeten' takes 'te' before the second verb: 'te drinken', with the infinitive at the end.
Dutch has no single word for 'would like'; it uses 'graag' with 'wil': 'graag wil ik'.
De-words keep the -e even after 'een': 'een zware doos', because 'doos' is a de-word.
A het-word takes -e when definite: 'het stille park'. Say 'een stil park' with no -e when indefinite.
The person receiving comes first, then the thing: 'wijst de nieuwe medewerker de weg', no 'aan' needed.
Mark the receiver with 'aan' after the object: 'het verhaal aan de kinderen'.
Days of the week take 'op': 'op woensdag' for 'on Wednesday'.
'Eraan gewend' splits: the 'er' moves up and 'aan' drops to the end, giving 'er al gewend aan'.
'Inschrijven' is separable: the prefix 'in' breaks off to the end, so 'schrijven ons in'.
'Opstijgen' splits in a main clause: 'op' lands at the very end, after 'stijgen'.
'Lang' can mean both 'long' and 'tall' in Dutch – context makes it clear.
In the perfect, the participle closes the sentence: 'hebben ... gewerkt', with 'gewerkt' at the end.
'Aandacht schenken aan' is the fixed phrase for paying attention to: 'schenkt aandacht aan'.
After a linking verb like 'klinkt', the adjective takes no ending: 'klinkt heel mooi', no -e on 'mooi'.
After a verb like 'moet', Dutch can drop 'gaan' before a direction: 'moet ik ... naar kantoor' implies going.
'Laat ik ...' means 'let me ...', a set way to propose what you will do: 'laat ik beginnen'.
The time word ''s nachts' means 'at night': the 's is a leftover of old 'des', kept with the apostrophe.
Separable verbs put 'ge' in the middle of the past participle: 'uitstellen' becomes 'uitgesteld'.
A het-word drops the adjective -e after 'een': 'een groot huis', not 'grote'.
A change of state takes 'zijn' in the perfect, not 'hebben': 'zijn moe geworden'.
'Even' here means briefly or for a moment, softening 'houdt ... stil' to a short pause.
Motion to a destination takes 'zijn', not 'hebben', in the perfect: 'zijn ... gereden'.
Material adjectives like 'glazen' end in -en and never change form: 'een glazen vaas'.
'Vallen' uses 'zijn' in the perfect, not 'hebben': 'is gevallen' for the completed action.
'Nauwelijks' paired with a later 'of' means barely had X happened when Y: 'nauwelijks was ik thuis of de telefoon ging'.
Weather uses a dummy 'het' as subject: 'is het koud', literally 'is it cold'.
'Niet tegen iets kunnen' means can't stand something: 'kan niet tegen de kou'.
After a verb like 'wil', the separable verb stays whole as an infinitive: 'wil ... inruilen', not split.
